title: Knowledge
reviewNotes: Complete four-piece diagram after ...Kxd8 visually re-reviewed with the source’s explicit Q castling stipulation. Three branches check O-O-O+/Kc7/Kxb2, independent ...Rd2/Rxd2+ and the drawing Rd1+/Kc7 comparison. A legal winning-move proof links the rights-bearing root to the exact opponent loss after castling; the root is not directly tablebase-probed. Earlier d7/promotion sacrifice choices remain outside scope.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players might make a draw, but only a true genius would be able to win from this position. You see, it seems evident that white is playing for a win, being the only one left with an extra pawn that is only two squares away from getting a new queen. But actually, things are not as simple as they might seem. If we try to push this pawn, now after king to c7, the king is defending the promotion square. If we go behind with the rook, the king is actually going to step in front of the pawn, and there is no easy way to kick him out. This rook is going to come around and collect the pawn. >> [music] >> So, what happens if we defend the pawn naturally, like this? Again, the king goes in front, and if you give a check, it's now going to collect the pawn. There is no progress to be made. So, pushing the pawn directly doesn't seem to work. What about rook to d1, defending the pawn first? Well, now black can play rook to h2 and prepare to skewer the rook, so that now after the king moves, black is going to collect the rook while [music] defending the promotion square. And if we take the rook, now the black king is in time to stop the pawn. But if instead of pushing the pawn right away, we try to play, for example, rook to d3, maintaining the rook, now we give black enough time to run back to the back rank and stop the pawn from in front of it. So, is this it? Is this position just a draw? Well, not exactly. You see, there is one little detail that I kind of forgot to mention, but in my defense, I'm pretty sure you didn't ask about it. White is winning, and the first move is indeed pawn to d7. This doesn't seem to make sense. The king goes to c7, defends the promotion, and attacks the pawn. How can this be winning? Well, let me show you the next move, and I'm sure that it will make a lot of sense. The only winning move in this position is to promote the pawn. A ridiculous and preposterous sacrifice. We are giving up the only advantage we had on black and yet the key to winning this position is knowledge. And the knowledge that we are missing is the fact that this king and this rook have not moved for the entirety of this game, which is something that you could not know by just looking at the starting position, but it is something that you have to consider a possibility. And so indeed after long castles this is a check to the black king and the white king [music] is attacking the rook. And yes, it is legal to castle because the white king is not passing through check. So, after this move the black king will have to move. White will collect the black rook and win the game.
